How Europe’s green hydrogen ambitions could keep Tunisia’s worst polluter alive
Submitted by
Francesco Torri
on
Tue, 11/17/2026 - 11:13
A German-backed plan sold as a clean energy transition is seen by many Tunisians as a lifeline for a heavily polluting phosphate industry
Smoke billows from the chimney of a section of the state-run phosphate processing plant in the southern city of Gabes on 31 October 2025 (Fethi Belaid/AFP)
Off
As
Tunisia
’s green hydrogen strategy is being promoted as a cornerstone of Europe’s clean energy transition, residents in the southern city of Gabes argue it could instead extend the life of one of the country’s most polluting industrial complexes while increasing pressure on scarce resources.
On 21 October 2025, around 100,000 people
marched
through Gabes in one of the largest environmental
protests
North Africa
has seen in years. Demonstrators demanded the closure of the Groupe Chimique Tunisien (GCT), the state-owned phosphate complex that has polluted the city’s air and sea for decades.
Residents also mobilised against plans to decarbonise the GCT and turn it into a green hydrogen hub supplying Europe. Critics describe the project as a form of “green colonialism”, saying Tunisia would bear the environmental costs while Europe reaps most of the benefits.
Germany, which expects to import
50 to 70 percent
of its hydrogen demand by 2030, has been the leading force behind Tunisia’s National Green Hydrogen Strategy,
published
in July 2024. Berlin financed the strategy and provided the technical expertise behind its design through GIZ’s
H2Vert.TUN
project.
As the strategy itself states, Tunisia aims to produce 8.3 million tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2050. Of that total, only around 2 million tonnes would remain in the country. The strategy identifies the production of green ammonia at the GCT’s Gabes complex as the main and earliest domestic use planned for green hydrogen in Tunisia, while most of the remaining output would be exported to Europe.
Green hydrogen would replace the fossil hydrogen the GCT uses to produce ammonia for fertilisers and reduce its carbon emissions. But this “decarbonisation” would do nothing to address the plant’s other major sources of pollution, including sulphur dioxide, fluorides and phosphogypsum, which have contaminated the environment for decades and continue to
make Gabes’ residents sick.
The hydrogen is expected to be exported to Europe through the
EU-backed
SoutH2 Corridor
. In parallel, Brussels
pledged
€35.4m ($38.9m) for Tunisia’s renewable energy infrastructure, while
agreements
signed with energy multinationals envisaged €120bn in private investment.
Yet little progress has followed.
“Everybody is waiting for something to develop,” Edward Koenen, head of finance and sales at ABO Energy, one of the companies that signed a memorandum of understanding, told Middle East Eye.
“The Tunisian government said they are not that interested in constructing anything, because there is no market for green hydrogen.”
Officially, Tunis has not changed course. On 1 October, it reaffirmed its commitment to the SoutH2 pipeline project by signing the
Algiers Ministerial Declaration
, but nothing has progressed beyond paper.
As the high costs associated with green hydrogen have become clearer, what some analysts once described as Europe’s “hydrogen hype” has begun to fade. In September 2025, the International Energy Agency cut its
2030 forecast
for low-emissions hydrogen production by a quarter.
No to ‘green facade’
However, according to Saber Ammar, a Tunisian activist and researcher at the Tunisian think tank Transnational Institute, there is another element behind Tunisia’s stall on its green hydrogen strategy: the opposition of Gabes’ residents and Tunisian civil society.
Opponents argue that the projects would primarily benefit European consumers while entrenching an industrial model that many residents of Gabes want dismantled.
“There was a coalition between the trade union, the social movement, the environmental justice movement, and we created some sort of an anti-green hydrogen front,” Saber told MEE.
‘Last year, starting from September, hundreds of people went to the hospital due to suffocation caused by the gases emitted by the industry’
- Islem Zrelli, member of Stop Pollution
One of the key components in this coalition is “Stop Pollution”, an environmental movement born in 2012 in Gabes to oppose the severe pollution and health impacts caused by the GCT.
Kheireddine Debia, one of Stop Pollution’s leaders, told MEE that what activists want "is to shut down the industrial complex, not to give it a green facade".
Debia
received
a six-month suspended sentence last month for protesting against the GCT, while nine other activists were
handed
prison terms of up to a year as part of a broader
crackdown
on dissent since President Kais Saied’s
power grab
in 2021.
Islem Zrelli, a young member of Stop Pollution, believes the GCT has already done too much damage. Last year’s protests erupted after more than 120 residents were hospitalised following severe gas leaks.
“Last year, starting from September, hundreds of people went to the hospital due to suffocation caused by the gases emitted by the industry,” he told MEE. “Many of them were kids and students from Chatt Essalem, my neighbourhood.”
Tunisia: Thousands protest in Gabes against chemical plant pollution
Read More »
The GCT’s phosphate processing and fertiliser production have caused long-term health problems among the population, including chronic respiratory illnesses. Its radioactive waste product,
phosphogypsum
, has been linked to higher cancer rates and has polluted the Gulf of Gabes, harming marine life and contaminating waters that residents rely on for their livelihoods and food.
In 2017, thanks to Stop Pollution’s mobilisation and civil society pressure, the government
promised
to dismantle the phosphate unit.
However, on 5 March 2025, a restricted ministerial council chaired by Prime Minister Kamel Maddouri
reversed course
. It removed phosphogypsum from Tunisia’s list of hazardous wastes, despite an estimated 70 million tonnes of the material having been dumped by the plant into the Mediterranean over the previous 25 years.
The controversial move is part of a 2025-2030 plan to
expand
phosphate production from under three million to 14 million tonnes a year. The council also approved the creation of pilot green ammonia units in Gabes, envisaged as the cornerstone of Tunisia’s domestic green hydrogen industry and a key component of the export-oriented hydrogen economy outlined in the German-backed national strategy.
For the people of Gabes, this means more phosphogypsum in the sea and higher emissions of toxic gases into the air, including ammonia, which a GCT audit
found
to be already exceeding permitted levels in 2025.
Green extractivism
Critics say Tunisia’s green hydrogen strategy could also carry significant social and economic costs.
“The problem is that green hydrogen needs fresh water, and Tunisia doesn’t have any fresh water,” Fadhel Kaboub, associate professor of economics at Denison University and president of the Global Institute for Sustainable Prosperity, told MEE.
“So the solution is desalination, and desalination plants produce the salt brine, which is chemically toxic for sea life, that is dumped usually in the ocean. It kills the blue economy.”
‘It is reminiscent of the fossil fuel system. And with green hydrogen, we risk reproducing that model, with more foreign debt’
- Hanen Keskes, Greenpeace MENA
The worsening water stress that environmentalists have warned about for years has already become a reality in Tunisia. This year, the country faced its
hottest summer on record
, with power cuts that stopped the water pumps and left towns without water for days, prompting protests across the country.
According to the Transnational Institute’s
analysis
of the strategy, exporting six million tonnes of green hydrogen would also require more than 90 gigawatts of solar and wind capacity covering 500,000 hectares, about 3 percent of Tunisia and roughly twice the area of Greater Tunis.
Most of it would be
concentrated
in a planned “hydrogen valley” in southern Tunisia, much of it on communal land used by local communities for herding and small-scale farming. The strategy, however, offers few details on how such land would be secured.
Since 2016, Tunisia has
loosened land laws
to open agricultural and collective land to energy investors. In villages such as Segdoud, collective land has already been
appropriated
by the state for solar projects without compensation, according to residents and rights advocates.
Moreover, while the
strategy
promises more than 400,000 jobs by 2050, a 2021
study
commissioned by GIZ warned that producing hydrogen with imported technology and exporting it as a raw material “would create limited jobs and value in Tunisia”. The study added that most of the jobs created would be temporary, tied to the construction of solar and wind projects.
Green hydrogen: The EU's new resource grab in North Africa
Read More »
Hamza Hamouchene, a founding member of the Environmental Justice North Africa (EJNA) network and programme coordinator at the Transnational Institute, argues that the strategy risks reproducing an extractivist economic model, where Europe profits from North Africa’s minimally processed resources while local communities see few lasting gains.
“Europe and its companies, what we call the Global North, want to continue to get their cheap natural resources, including green electricity and green hydrogen,” he told MEE. “Yet these projects end up not creating long-term, sustainable, good jobs for local populations.”
Officials estimate that producing every million tonnes of green hydrogen would
require
$25bn in investment, a cost they acknowledge Tunisia cannot bear alone. Critics warn that the strategy could lock the country into a new cycle of foreign debt, with public financing used to reduce risks for foreign investors.
“This is the built-in problem with extractivism, including green extractivism,” Hanen Keskes, political campaign lead at Greenpeace MENA, told MEE.
“You de-risk the European corporations through government loans, while just exporting raw, very depletable resources. It is reminiscent of the fossil fuel system. And with green hydrogen, we risk reproducing that model, with more foreign debt.”
Inside Tunisia
Achref Chibani
Jasper Humpert
Gabes, Tunisia

•

British businesses run by long-serving directors of the Bank of England profited from “brutal” enslavement in Cuba for decades after slavery’s abolition in the British empire, according to research.
Men and boys were enslaved in prison conditions at the El Cobre copper ore mine near Santiago de Cuba, which supplied British firms during the Industrial Revolution, the historian Chris Evans has found.

items.title: Morning update
items.content:
Morning update
Good Morning Middle East Eye readers,
If you are just joining us, here are key developments from across the region and beyond:
*Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says its forces attacked two US bases in Bahrain; Manama says strikes hit civilian industrial facility.
*The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen's Houthis towards Saudi Arabia's western region.
*Two Palestinians injured in an Israeli strike on Gaza succumb as territory's health ministry says death toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” rises to 1,661.
*Israeli settlers torched Palestinian-owned vehicles and spray-painted alleged racist graffiti on Palestinian homes in several West Bank villages.
*The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has urged Germany to arrest an Israeli soldier, Almog Keisi, who has been sighted in Luneburg this week, accusing him of war crimes, crimes against humanity and acts of genocide in Gaza.
*Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Israel is blocking thousands of container homes destined for Gaza, adding that Israeli authorities argue Hamas could use the metal structures  for manufacturing weapons.
*Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that his country was engaged in a "silent war that is far more difficult than the one in which missiles are launched and destruction is inflicted".
*Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused Iran of meddling in Lebanon's affairs through Hezbollah's weapons and also demanded Israel withdraw from the country's south.
*Pro-Israel US Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries has pledged to advance legislation targeting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank within the first 100 days of the new Congress.

items.title: Israeli settlers torch vehicles in West Bank, paint 'racist' graffiti on homes
items.content:
Israeli settlers torch vehicles in West Bank, paint 'racist' graffiti on homes
Israeli settlers set fire to 12 Palestinian-owned vehicles and spray-painted racist graffiti during attacks on three villages in Ramallah and al-Bireh in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian media reported.
Local sources told Wafa that a group of settlers attacked the village of Kafr Malik, east of Ramallah, setting fire to seven vehicles and spray-painting racist slogans on the walls of some homes.
In a separate attack, colonists raided the town of Deir Abu Mash'al, northwest of Ramallah, setting fire to three vehicles and spraying racist graffiti before fleeing the area.
In Deir al-Sudan, north of Ramallah, colonists set fire to two vehicles belonging to two Palestinian citizens, causing extensive material damage.
Israeli police, according to Haaretz, said they had opened an investigation into arson, graffiti and property damage at four sites in the West Bank.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned the attacks, calling them "Jewish terrorism" and warning that extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes were pushing the West Bank toward "anarchy."
Israeli settler militias set fire to several Palestinian vehicles in the village of Kafr Malik, east of Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, in the early hours of Sunday. https://t.co/Rvh60XZpXN

An explosion struck an ammunition depot inside a naval base in Libya's eastern port city of Benghazi on Sunday morning, local emergency authorities said, according to Al-Masar TV, a news channel.
The authorities have not disclosed the cause of the explosion or whether it caused any casualty. Emergency response teams were deployed to the military facility following the blast to contain the resulting fire.

items.title: At least 24 killed and dozens missing in confectionery factory fire in Indonesia
items.content:
Rescuers brave unstable structures in search for missing as DNA needed to identify victims
Indonesia has confirmed the deaths of 24 people in a fire that tore ⁠through a factory, as rescuers braved unstable structures in the burned wreckage to search for ⁠about 30 people ⁠still missing.
Authorities ​were still investigating the cause of the fire, which broke out on Saturday in the PT Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Cikande in Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta.

items.title: IRGC chief says Iran's air space 'red line' for armed forces
items.content:
IRGC chief says Iran's air space 'red line' for armed forces
Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) Major General Ahmad Vahidi has said that Iran’s airspace is a red line for the country's armed forces and any breach will be met with a "firm and decisive response", Mehr news agency reported.
On Saturday, Major General Vahidi visited Iran's underground missile city for the first time as the force unveiled a new dual-missile launcher.
During his visit, Vahidi said that "events unfolding for the enemy were only the beginning" and that "the enemy would witness humiliation and defeat and that truth would prevail over falsehood", according to Mehr.

items.content:
مباشر: البحرين تتهم إيران باستهداف "منشأة صناعية مدنية" والتحالف بقيادة السعودية يتصدى لهجمات حوثية
نشب حريق في منشأة صناعية بالبحرين جراء ضربة إيرانية السبت، وفق ما أعلنت المملكة التي استهدفتها أربعة هجومات منذ منتصف تشرين الثاني/نوفمبر، فيما تؤكّد طهران أنها تردّ على الضربات الأمريكية في ظلّ تصاعد حدّة النزاع في الشرق الأوسط. من جهته، أفاد ​التحالف الذي تقوده ​السعودية السبت بأنه اعترض ودمر ​صاروخا ‌باليستيا أطلقه الحوثيون باتجاه المنطقة ‌الغربية في المملكة، وسط تصاعد حدة التوتر بين السعودية والجماعة ​المتحالفة مع ‌إيران. تابعوا تغطيتنا المباشرة.

items.title: Israeli puts 'Gaza mosque crescent finial' up for sale, rights group says
items.content:
Israeli puts 'Gaza mosque crescent finial' up for sale, rights group says
An Israeli rights group has shared an image of an Israeli offering for sale a purported crescent finial from a mosque in Gaza's Rafah crossing.
In a post on X, Mistaclim said "a pious Jew" trades "in loot, in the spoils of war".
"Offers for sale for 2,500 shekels the moon at the end of the central mosque in the Rafah crossing and boasts that he has proof," the post read.
"And perhaps the problem lies in the rotten Israeli society, where the destruction of a place of worship is an opportunity for 'pride in the living room'."

items.content:
Kraftwerk Berlin, part of same development as techno club Tresor, transformed into ‘war room’ for arms firm event
With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.
On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.

items.title: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
items.content:
As nationalist, Eurosceptic parties surge in four of the bloc’s biggest member states, the coming year’s polls could test its resilience like never before
In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.
Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.

items.title: World Central Kitchen founder says three killed in Gaza strike 'not part of our team'
items.content:
World Central Kitchen founder says three killed in Gaza strike 'not part of our team'
The founder of the World Central Kitchen, Jose Andres, has said that the three people killed in an Israeli strike on a vehicle delivering food aid in Gaza, did not belong the organisation, nor did the vehicle.
In a post on X, Andres said, "Early reports linked them to World Central Kitchen. They were not part of our team, and it was not our vehicle. That's all we know."
"But here is what I do know. More than a year into a ceasefire, people in Gaza are still dying. Families are facing a fourth winter in tents," he added.
The Israeli army had earlier claimed in a post on X that it targeted three “Islamic Jihad terrorists” in a vehicle used to transport food and supplies to other group operatives in Gaza.
Andres added that a "ceasefire is not peace", calling upon leaders to work towards ending the conflict.
"To every leader with the power to change this, on every side: finish the work. End this war for good, so Palestinians and Israelis can live in safety, and so the people of Gaza can start to rebuild their homes, their schools, their kitchens," he said.
"Our teams, Gazans feeding Gazans, were cooking again today. They will be there tomorrow. A plate of food is hope. But it is not a future. Peace is."

items.title: Pro-Israel Hakeem Jeffries says he will push legislation targeting settler violence
items.content:
Pro-Israel Hakeem Jeffries says he will push legislation targeting settler violence
Pro-Israel US Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House of Representatives next year, has pledged to advance legislation targeting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank within the first 100 days of the new Congress.
In an interview with The New York Times, Jeffries said the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act should be among the early legislative priorities, adding that he expected strong support for it within the House Democratic Caucus.
Jeffries also described the devastation inflicted on Palestinian civilians in Gaza as “unacceptable, unsustainable and un-American”, calling for increased humanitarian assistance, medical aid, housing support and access to clean water and air.
Asked whether he supported the proposed Block the Bombs and Stop the Settlements bills, which call for restricting arms sale to Israel and broader sanctions on settlement expansion, Jeffries said he had not taken a position.
On calls to halt US weapons exports used in regional conflicts, he said the current approach was “not sustainable” and needed to change.
More than a million people have signed a petition urging Democrats to reject Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the US House of Representative. An Economist/YouGov poll published last month found that Jeffries had just a 26 percent approval rating among registered voters.
Critics say that one reason Jeffries' popularity has taken a hit is that he is an avid supporter of Israel.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) ranks among his top campaign-financing contributors.
Jeffries said he expects strong support for the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act. (AFP)

items.title: Former UN envoy says Iran war was 'perfectly avoidable'
items.content:
Former UN envoy says Iran war was 'perfectly avoidable'
Iran war could have been avoided, Álvaro de Soto, a former UN special coordinator for the Middle East peace process, has said.
“It was perfectly avoidable. It need not have happened,” he said, adding that US officials have offered differing explanations for going to war.
Speaking at MED Dialogues conference in Naples, he said: “Lasting peace requires a willingness to confront the problems at the root of a conflict. Without addressing them, opportunities for peace will continue to be missed.”

items.title: Turkey says Israel could use Druze support to launch Syria operation
items.content:
Turkey says Israel could use Druze support to launch Syria operation
Israeli could use its support of the Druze to launch an operation in Syria, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said, warning that such an attack could lead to a wider conflict in the region.
In an interview with Turkish media, Fidan said Israel is providing military equipment and support to a Druze tribe in Syria, and may use that support to provoke the Syrian army and launch an attack.
Fidan said Turkey has discussed such the possibility of this operation with European and American officials.
The violence last year in Druze-majority Sweida - which began with clashes between Druze factions and Bedouin fighters in the southern province - left more than 2,000 people dead, including 789 Druze civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights.
The Sweida violence also saw Israel launching air strikes in the province as well as in the capital Damascus, nominally in support of the Druze minority. In August, it struck a Syrian airbase where it said Turkey was planning to deploy forces.

items.title: Bahrain says Iran struck industrial site as tankers hit in Hormuz
items.content:
Bahrain accused Iran of striking a civilian industrial facility on Saturday, causing a fire and damage but no casualties, while two tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the Middle East conflict.
The Gulf kingdom has suffered several attacks this week, ending a weeks-long lull in the conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
